**The Colors of Memory**

*When I think about the past, it’s not the facts that return to me first.*
It’s the *sensations*—the flicker of a neon sign against the humid night, the exact smell of rain hitting hot pavement, the way my grandmother’s hands smelled like soap and warm biscits. These fragments don’t come to me in words at first. They come like brushstrokes—a sudden splash of yellow in the corner of my eye, the guttural rumble of a bus engine passing too close. I have to sit with them before they morph into memories I can name.

I’ve always envied people who remember dates. Birthdays, anniversaries, the exact year something happened. I don’t. My memory is a collage of impressions left behind by time, like a sheet of paper that’s been folded too many times—some cracks are deliberate and easy to trace, others split invisibly, and the only way to find them is to press your fingers along the edges until one finally gives under your touch.

---

*Does memory even belong to us?*

That’s the question that wakes me up at 3 AM sometimes. Not the philosophical kind with easy answers, but the raw, creeping dread that comes with realizing how little control we have over what lingers. Just last week, I opened a box of old photographs—ones I hadn’t seen in years—and there, staring back at me from a yellowing Polaroid, was a girl I didn’t recognize. Brown eyes blinking too wide, grinning under a fringe of bangs she must have envied (she tied yarn around them with desperate hope, once). I knew it was me at twelve. I *knew* it. And yet, looking at her was like staring at a stranger through a fogged-up window. I raised a hand to touch the photo, half-expecting the glass to be cold, to belong to someone else entirely.

That’s the lie we tell ourselves—that the past is something we revisit, like a house we left and can come back to. But memory isn’t a place. It’s a *sensation*, a ghost of what we were, replayed in flickers. By the time I close the photo box and set it back in the closet, the girl’s face is already fading again. Maybe I’ll hold onto that image a little longer. Maybe in a week, it’ll slide entirely back into the dark.

---

*I was six the first time I realized lies could be beautiful.*

It was a summer evening in my childhood town, where fireflies clung to the tops of grass like tiny burning questions. My father had promised to take me fishing, but he forgot. Instead, he sat me down on the porch steps and told me, with complete sincerity, that the fireflies were “fairy lanterns” that only appeared when someone very kind did good deeds for others. He pointed to my neighbor’s yard, where Mrs. Holloway—who always gave me butterscotch candies when she saw me pass—was watering her roses. “See? She’s kind. That’s why they’re out tonight.”

I believed him. For weeks after, I tried to catch one so I could know, *really* know, that what he’d said was true. I’d put my palm over them in jars until my mother caught me and gasped in horror. (That jar has its own place in my memory, too—the scent of trapped green, the sting of my mother’s voice rewiring my faith in the magical voice of adults.)

Years later, when I told my father about it—the way he’d tricked me so effortlessly—he laughed. “It was too pretty a story not to share,” he said. I didn’t laugh back. Something in me recoiled. Not because he was wrong—*Truth is sometimes impossible for children*, he later amended—but because he hadn’t seen the betrayal in the way I did. It wasn’t about the fireflies. It was about the way he’d said “kind” like it was a currency I could spend, as if goodness was something he could trade me for in sugar-dipped lies.

I stopped believing in fairy lanterns after that.

But sometimes, I still wonder if the fireflies ever came when no one was watching.

---

*The things we repeat to ourselves are anchors. Some hold. Some drag.*

I was twelve when I first cut myself. It wasn’t for the reasons people usually assume—pain so deep there wasn’t language for it, voices demanding I quiet them in the only way I knew. It was something sneakier. A quiet experiment. Would the body remember what the mind couldn’t?

I thought I’d feel more. But it was just a line of blood, thin as a comma, and after a while, the scar faded. The story didn’t. Sometimes, when I’m tired, a shadow lingers along my forearm, ghosting over the old wound. It’s not pain. It’s nostalgia. A memory of a self who thought she could control the chaos inside by carving it out.

I don’t know if the body ever forgets what the mind tries to erase. The scar is still there. Faint, but present. Like the way I still tense when someone walks up behind me too fast, even though I’ve lived my whole life in places where no one would hurt me.

The mind holds onto safety in the same way it holds onto trauma. It’s just a different kind of hunger.

---

*I’ve been avoiding this.*

(See? There it is again—the way memory sneaks up like a cat napping in the sun, then pounces when you’re not looking. I’m doing it now, touching on something I swore I wouldn’t relive.)

Three years ago, I found out my mother was sick. The diagnosis came in a series of calls, each one a step further into the labyrinth of medical terms and statistics that made my hands shake. I didn’t cry at first. I just sat there, staring at the wallpaper in my apartment—a peeling floral pattern I’d picked years ago because I liked the way it made the walls feel softer. I remember thinking: *This is happening. This is happening.* Like I was observing it from outside myself.

Later that night, I called my best friend and said, “I’m going home.” I don’t know why I phrased it like that—like home was a place she had to give me permission to return to. But when I arrived, everything smelled the same—the lemon-scented cleaner she used, the faintest hint of cigarette smoke she’d never quite manage to wash out of her clothes. I tried not to breathe too deep.

The first time I saw her after the chemo started, she’d lost her hair. Not all of it—just enough that she looked like she’d been in a fight with the wind and lost. She showed me her bald spots with this strange pride, pulling back her headscarf like it was a veil revealing a secret treasure. “Look at me,” she said, smiling. “I look like an alien. Like something out of *Star Trek*.”

I laughed. But later, when she was asleep, I traced the outline of her hand with my finger. Her skin was paper-thin. Her nail polish—she’d insisted on painting her nails bright red—was chipped at the edges, like she’d been chewing on them. I put my own hands next to hers on the bedspread and felt the weight of time between them. A whole lifetime, condensed into two sets of fingers, one grown, one still learning how to be.

---

*The body keeps the score.*

I didn’t know what that meant until I sat in the chemotherapy room with her, watching the clear liquid drip from the IV into her veins. The room was full of the sounds of people pretending not to listen to sobs, of machines beeping in rhythm that felt like a clock counting down the seconds she had left. It smelled like antiseptic and despair.

I held her hand the whole time. She squeezed back when she could, but some of the time, her grip was weak, and I couldn’t tell if she was asleep or just too tired to respond. I kept thinking: *What if this is the last time I touch her?* The thought wasn’t dramatic. It was matter-of-fact. I knew too well how fragile the body is when it’s trying to survive something it can’t fight alone.

She came out of it. Mostly. Some days, she was herself again. She’d cook dinner and pretend the cancer was a minor inconvenience, just another bad episode of a TV show she’d binge-watched. Other days, she couldn’t get out of bed. Then she’d just look at me with these eyes that were both full of apology and infinite patience, like I was the one who needed consoling.

I don’t know how people survive this. Not just the person with the illness, but the people who love them and can’t fix it. I’d give anything to say I bore it with grace. But the truth is, I wasn’t graceful. I was angry. I hated the machine that made her sick. I hated the part of me that wanted to scream at God or the universe or whatever cruel trickster had decided to flip the switch on her body.

Still, I kept going back.

---

*Grief is a shape-shifter.*

It doesn’t just sit in one place waiting for you to find it.
It gets up and dances with you.
It hums along to the radio in your car.
It cries in the shower where the noise of the water drowns everything else out.
It sits on the edge of your bed at 2 AM and whispers: *Remember?*

After she died, I tried to fill the space she left with noise. I traveled. I worked eighty hours a week. I avoided every room in my house that held even the faintest scent of her. I even stopped cooking because the smell of food made my stomach twist.

Then, one evening, I walked into a café and caught the scent of lavender—just a hint, the kind from a sachet someone had tucked into a handbag years ago and never replaced. I froze. My breath hitched. The world narrowed to that one smell, and suddenly I was ten years old again, standing in her kitchen while she taught me how to make pie crust. Her hands, dusted with flour, shaping the dough like it was something alive.

I didn’t cry right away. I just stood there, paralyzed, while the lavender smell grew stronger in my mind’s nose than it ever had in reality. It was almost too much to take. And then—it faded. Just like that. The café banality returned. The barista asked if I was alright.

I said I was.

(But the lie was beautiful.)

---

*I think this is why we hold onto objects—the ones that don’t matter to anyone else.*

Like the jar of buttons my grandmother left me. An odd collection—buttons from hats, clothes, curtains, each one different, but all of them the same in that they were *hers*. I’ve never sewn in my life. I don’t know what any of them were for. And yet, if I open that jar now, at 3 AM like I often do, the scent of old fabric and dust rises up, and suddenly I’m eight years old again, sitting at her sewing table while she hums show tunes and lets me play with the scraps of button-covered dress fabric she saved.

Or the keychain from my first job at the movie theater. A green laminated thing shaped like a reel-to-reel filmstrip, with the year 1998 stamped on it. I haven’t thought about that job in years. I flunked out of it after two weeks because I couldn’t figure out how to open the popcorn machine without spilling kernels everywhere. But there it is—on my desk right now. I don’t know why I keep it, except that it’s part of a story. One that doesn’t involve me being particularly competent, but one that involves *me*. And that, in the end, is enough.

Objects are liars. They promise us that if we only keep enough of them, we can stitch our lives back together again. But they also trick us into believing that the past is somewhere we can visit.

It’s not.

---

*I keep thinking about the way time works—how it can stretch and contract like taffy.*

You’re waiting for a bus in the rain, and it takes twelve years to arrive.
You fall in love, and suddenly it’s like the universe paused for two whole summers just so you could exist in that feeling.
You grieve someone you love, and the world keeps moving like nothing’s changed, even though you’re frozen in amber eighteen months ago.

I hate that the past feels like a country I’ve been exiled from. I hate that places I loved—her kitchen, my childhood home, even a stretch of highway that used to take me somewhere magical—are now physical ghosts. I hate that memory is a currency I have to spend carefully, because every time I indulge it, it feels like I’m cheating on the present.

But.

But.

If I could go back and tell my six-year-old self anything, it wouldn’t be to warn her about the fairy lanterns. It would be to say: *You will forget the words, but not the weight. You will lose people you love, but you will carry their hands in yours long after they’re gone. You will make mistakes that feel unforgivable, but the most important thing is that you keep having feelings—even when they hurt.*

And if I could whisper to the me who found out about the cancer—*You will survive it. You will survive the grief. You will carry her inside you like a constellation of scars that will always tell your story.*

---

*I don’t know how to end this.*

Memories don’t wrap up neatly. They don’t come with morals or punchlines. They just fade, or they stay stubborn, or they rewrite themselves in the dark until you don’t know if you’re remembering what happened, or what you wished would have.

So instead of an ending, I’ll give you this:

If you press your palm against your chest right now and close your eyes, you might feel something beating back at you.

It’s not just your heart.
It’s all the people you’ve loved.
All the versions of you that have ever existed.
All the ghosts of everything that’s ever left a mark.

And they’re still with you.

Even when you forget their names,
even when you stop believing in fairy lanterns,
even when the keys to your past rattle in a jar you’ll never open again—
